title: AegisFlow: A Multi-Agent Agentic AI Framework for Autonomous Remediation and Self-Healing in Fragile Data Ecosystems
authors: Muhammad Bilal Awan; Zubair Hussain; Abdul Shahid
central_claim: Data-pipeline self-healing loop: a Watchdog detects exceptions and silent semantic drift (KS tests, null-frequency, range violations that flag unit changes, type checks); a Repair agent diffs failed vs successful upstream responses, synthesizes an LLM patch, validates it on 10 recent snapshots against success invariants in a digital-twin sandbox, then auto-commits and blue-green deploys (human review only for 70-80% pass rates) and monitors the next 100 runs with rollback.
cite_claim: A 2026 system closes a detect-silent-drift -> LLM patch -> sandbox-validate -> deploy loop for data pipelines broken by upstream API/schema drift, but deploys autonomously without a committed reproduction test or a PR.
location: Sec. 4 'Watchdog Agent', 'Repair Agent', 'Shadow Sandbox', 'Hot-Swap Deployer'; Sec. 6 'Experimental Setup' (PDF text, read 2026-10-21)
quote: Range violation detection identifies values outside expected min/max bounds derived from historical data, flagging unit changes or data corruption.
relevance: Strongest new research counter-example to the combination claim: silent-drift trigger + upstream-response diff + patch + invariant-gated validation + post-deploy confirmation. Differs: batch-statistical (not per-call contract), no F-gated committed test, no PR/never-merge, no agent receipt, not MCP. Quality caveats: no code; evaluation dates inconsistent ('January - March 2016'); production claims unverifiable.

title: How we verify Cleric’s production fixes
central_claim: A separate verifier agent per issue generates check code, reruns it on a schedule, and decides whether the defect (not just the alert) is gone after a fix; outcome data show recurring alert clusters disappear more often after an applied fix than without one.
cite_claim: An AI-SRE vendor already measures recurrence after an applied fix versus no fix (64% vs 22% of recurring alert clusters disappeared; daily recurrence 18% -> 7%).
location: Sections 'Checks are generated for each issue but run outside the agent' and 'What the outcome data revealed'
quote: 64% of recurring alert clusters disappeared completely from our data after a fix was applied, compared to 22% when the fix was not applied.
relevance: Weakens fiks's measurement-novelty claim 'recurrence after repair vs detection-only nobody reports': a vendor reports a fix-vs-no-fix recurrence comparison (observational, vendor-run, no CIs). fiks's version must be framed as controlled, per-contract, across agents and seeds.

title: Cleric product: Catch failures before your customers do
central_claim: Cleric records per-change production expectations (e.g., p95 latency, retry rate), compares them with observed behaviour for up to 14 days, opens a fix PR when an expectation is not met, and confirms recovery after the fix deploys.
cite_claim: Commercial AI-SRE products trigger on unmet production expectations for a change, open fix PRs, and confirm recovery after deploy.
quote: Cleric flags the regression in the change’s Slack or Microsoft Teams channel, opens a fix PR, and confirms recovery once the fix deploys.
relevance: Matrix row: Sem P (aggregate metric expectations, not per-result values), PR Y, Conf Y. Trigger is a metric deviation after the team's own deploy, not upstream drift seen in a successful tool result; no repro test or pre-PR gate described.

title: LangSmith Cloud changelog (weeks of Oct 5-12 and Oct 12-19, 2026)
central_claim: October 2026 Engine updates: PR-merge markers on recurrence charts to show whether recurrences stopped after a fix; Done issues reopen on recurrence; issue validation replays each source run against the fix preview deployment; Engine watches CI on its own PRs and pushes up to three revisions; fix PRs now open ready for review.
cite_claim: As of October 2026, LangSmith Engine replays source runs against a fix preview deployment and charts recurrence around the merged fix PR, i.e., it now has replay-based validation and post-merge confirmation.
quote: Issue charts now mark when each fix's pull request merged, drawing a dashed line labeled PR #N on the recurrence and metric charts
relevance: Moves Engine's Conf cell from P to Y and Gates/F toward P (model-judged replay, not a committed deterministic test; CI iterated after the PR exists). Extends [langsmith-changelog-2026] (Sep 2026 successful-tool-result reading). Engine repairs agent code, not the tool's repository.

title: Devin Oncall
central_claim: Responders watch Slack/Teams alert channels and PagerDuty incidents; for alerts Devin finds root cause and mitigation, for bug reports it reproduces the issue and fixes it in code; Oncall opens fix PRs and reports summarize PRs opened and merged.
cite_claim: Coding agents now start automatically from monitoring alerts and incidents and open fix PRs.
quote: Devin starts as soon as an alert, bug report, or incident fires, and uses your telemetry, code, deployments, runbooks, and past incidents
relevance: Alert-triggered coding agent (cluster E). Triggers are loud signals (alerts, incidents, bug reports); 'reproducing the issue' is stated for bug reports, but no committed fail-first test or pre-PR gate is documented.

title: Automations (Devin)
central_claim: Event-driven automations start Devin sessions from Slack, GitHub, Linear, PagerDuty, schedules and custom webhooks; any external system (Datadog, Sentry, custom tools) can POST to a webhook whose payload becomes the session prompt.
cite_claim: Any detector can be wired to an autonomous coding agent through a generic webhook trigger.
quote: Wire any external system (PagerDuty, Datadog, Sentry, custom tools) to Devin via a webhook URL
relevance: Makes the 'composable baseline' concrete: a contract monitor + webhook + Devin/Cursor approximates fiks's loop minus the F gate and pre-PR gates. fiks must beat this composition (trace-vs-prose arm).

title: Automations (Cursor cloud agents)
central_claim: Cursor Automations run cloud agents on schedules or events from GitHub (incl. CI completed), Slack, Linear, Sentry (issue created), PagerDuty (incident triggered) and private webhooks; cloud agents can build and test and open PRs.
cite_claim: Commercial coding agents can be triggered by Sentry issues, PagerDuty incidents or arbitrary monitoring webhooks.
quote: You can use webhooks to connect automations to internal systems, CI pipelines, monitoring tools, and more.
relevance: Same cluster as Devin. Generic orchestration; no semantic checker, repro gate or pre-PR gate of its own. Marketplace template 'Investigate Sentry issues' is error-triggered.

title: Cloud Agents (Cursor)
central_claim: Cloud agents run in their own VM, can build/test the changed software and open merge-ready PRs; started from Slack, Linear, GitHub/Bitbucket comments, API, web or desktop.
cite_claim: Background coding agents test in a VM and open PRs.
quote: Cloud agents produce merge-ready PRs with artifacts to demo their changes.
relevance: Repair-arm substitute for fiks (Fix/PR) but no trigger of its own.

title: About GitHub Copilot coding agent
central_claim: Copilot coding agent takes tasks from issues, PRs, the agents panel or chat integrations, runs tests and linters in an ephemeral environment, and opens one PR per task.
cite_claim: GitHub's coding agent is task/issue-triggered and can run tests and linters before a human reviews its PR.
quote: run tests and linters in an ephemeral cloud development environment
relevance: Repair arm only; any monitor that files an issue can trigger it. No monitor trigger on the page itself.

title: Overview of Azure SRE Agent
central_claim: On alerts from Azure Monitor, PagerDuty or ServiceNow, the agent correlates telemetry and deployments, hypothesizes root cause and proposes or (in Autonomous mode) executes mitigations such as restarts or scaling.
cite_claim: Hyperscaler SRE agents go from alerts to root cause and operational mitigations, with approval modes.
location: 'What you can do'; 'Handle an incident' tab
quote: On alert, the agent queries your monitoring tools, correlates signals across systems, identifies probable root cause, and proposes mitigations.
relevance: Ops mitigation, not code repair; its GitHub connector can open/merge PRs (see azure-sre-agent-github).

title: GitHub connector in Azure SRE Agent
central_claim: The connector lets the SRE agent search code, correlate errors to source lines, create issues, open and merge PRs and trigger workflows.
cite_claim: Azure SRE Agent can open and even merge PRs through its GitHub connector.
location: 'How your agent uses the GitHub connector' table
quote: Create/list issues, open/merge PRs, trigger and track GitHub Actions workflows
relevance: Note 'merge' capability: contrasts with fiks's never-merge rule. No repro-test or semantic trigger.

title: Coding Agents (Sentry integrations)
central_claim: Seer's root cause analysis can be handed to Claude, Cursor or GitHub Copilot agents for fix generation and PR creation.
cite_claim: Error-tracking vendors hand their RCA to third-party coding agents that open PRs.
quote: Seer's root cause analysis can be sent directly to the agent for automated fix generation and pull request creation.
relevance: Extends [sentry-seer-issue-fix] (C27): error-triggered; shows the 'detector -> any coding agent -> PR' pattern is standard.

title: AI Agents | PagerDuty
central_claim: PagerDuty's SRE Agent detects, triages and diagnoses incidents and performs approved remediation; the page does not mention code changes or PRs.
cite_claim: Incident-management AI agents remediate operationally with approval; code PRs are not described.
quote: Detects, triages, diagnoses incidents and performs approved remediation.
relevance: Negative for code repair; included to bound cluster E.

title: Acumen (Workato AIRO)
central_claim: Acumen monitors Workato automations and raises incidents for 'silent failures' (jobs stop processing without an error) and failure patterns, tracing root cause; no automated code repair is described.
cite_claim: Integration platforms now detect 'silent failures', but define them as stalls (no jobs) rather than wrong values, and stop at incidents and diagnosis.
quote: Silent failures — when an automation suddenly stops processing jobs even though no error has been thrown
relevance: Shows 'silent failure' is used in the connector-maintenance market with a narrower meaning; no repair loop.

title: How Hooks Work (Contextual Access)
central_claim: Arcade invokes external webhooks at access, pre-execution and post-execution points; the post-execution hook can allow, deny or modify a tool's output.
cite_claim: Agent-tool platforms expose a post-execution hook that could host a contract check, but document it for PII redaction and filtering.
quote: Allow, deny, or modify the result (output and content blocks). Use it to redact PII or filter content.
relevance: Portability host for fiks's Observe step (like Docker/ContextForge). Hook only; no semantic contracts shipped.

title: Tool executions
central_claim: Arcade records every tool execution with inputs and outputs (admin-only) and gives a manual triage table that attributes 'output is wrong or empty' to the tool's own logic.
cite_claim: A managed tool platform acknowledges wrong-but-successful tool outputs and leaves diagnosis to humans reading recorded inputs/outputs.
location: Triage table under 'Find a run in the dashboard' (two table cells joined with |)
quote: Inputs look right, output is wrong or empty | The tool’s own logic
relevance: Industry evidence that the silent wrong-output class is recognized and handled manually (supports C10-style claims).

title: Testing integrations
central_claim: Nango integration functions are tested with dry runs against live connections, recorded API responses saved as mocks, Vitest snapshot tests, and optional input/output schema validation.
cite_claim: Integration platforms already turn recorded upstream API responses into reproducible Vitest fixtures, developer-initiated.
quote: Mocks: Save API responses during dry runs to create reproducible test fixtures
relevance: Prior art for fiks's fixture mechanism (Repro P); not triggered by a runtime violation and not fail-first.

title: Breaking change detection
central_claim: Enterprise CI feature that flags unintentional breaking changes before SDKs and MCP tools are released.
cite_claim: SDK/MCP generators detect breaking changes in CI from the provider's side, before release.
quote: Stainless can automatically identify and flag unintentional breaking changes during your continuous integration (CI) process
relevance: Spec/CI-time, provider-side (C27 cluster). Cannot see a behavioural change that keeps the spec.

title: Toolkit versioning migration
central_claim: Since Python SDK v0.9.0 / TS v0.2.0, manual tool execution requires an explicit toolkit version; calls without one fail.
cite_claim: Managed toolkit vendors version their tools and require clients to pin versions, i.e., vendor-side tool changes are a recognized risk.
quote: Starting with Python SDK v0.9.0 and TypeScript SDK v0.2.0, manual tool execution requires explicit version specification.
relevance: Composio's public docs document versioning, not the 'tools that fix themselves' mechanism of [composio-mcp-gateway]; mechanism remains undocumented.

title: Systems and Methods for Detecting Silent Backward-Incompatible API Contract Drift Using Runtime Structural-Semantic Fingerprints
venue_or_publisher: Technical Disclosure Commons, Defensive Publications Series 10178 (2026-05-19)
central_claim: Learns endpoint invariants from production traffic, fingerprints responses and outputs drift alerts. Landing-page abstract mentions only detection and alerts; full PDF is behind a bot challenge and was not read.
cite_claim: A 2026 defensive publication describes traffic-learned silent-drift detection with alert output [abstract only; body not read].
location: Landing-page abstract (re-fetched 2026-10-21); PDF returned HTTP 403 (Cloudflare challenge) [verify]
quote: detecting backward-incompatible drift conditions, and outputting drift alerts characterizing the detected drift conditions.
relevance: Task (b) asked for a full-text check; it could not be done without bypassing bot detection. The abstract-level reading (detection + alerts only) stands but is marked [verify].

title: Beyond Fail-to-Pass: Iterative Hardening of Co-Generated Bug Reproduction Tests and Fixes
authors: Yuhao Tan; Zhibang Yang; Fangkai Yang; Yuan Yao; Yu Kang; Lu Wang et al.
central_claim: F->P is insufficient: 'lax' F->P reproduction tests admit plausible-but-incorrect patches (measured with mutation patches of the golden fix) and give no repair gain, while 'rigorous' ones add +8.5 pts; co-generated tests and fixes fail jointly 19.9% vs 10.6% expected; CoHarden writes the test before any fix and hardens it, reaching 69.4% resolved on SWE-bench Verified.
cite_claim: Passing a fail-to-pass check does not make a reproduction test strong enough; lax F->P tests admit plausible-but-incorrect patches and add no repair gain.
quote: some F->P BRTs are lax, reproducing the observed symptom yet still admitting plausible-but-incorrect patches.
relevance: Directly bears on fiks's F gate: supports the stated-reason gate and test-before-fix ordering, and supplies a measurable critique (laxity) that fiks's gate must answer. Gives an implementable metric (mutation-patch laxity).

title: Self-Healing Harness for Runtime Oversight of Agent Self-Modification
authors: Sina Tayebati; Divake Kumar; Nastaran Darabi; Ranganath Krishnan; Amit Ranjan Trivedi
central_claim: Admission gate for agent self-modifications (text rules): persist only after improvement on the triggering failure without regression on protected cases; 211 of 383 replay-rejected proposals (55%) fixed their trigger but broke a previously working case.
cite_claim: Over half of gate-rejected fixes improved their triggering failure while regressing a protected case.
quote: Of these, 211 (55%) improved their triggering failure while degrading a case that previously worked.
relevance: Empirical support for fiks's 'all stored traces + full contract suite' gate (C20 analogue), though on instruction rules, not code.

title: Do Agent Benchmarks Do What They Say? An Executable-Contract Audit of Tool-Using Agent Environments
authors: Rohith Reddy Bellibatlu; Zichong Wang; Wenbin Zhang
central_claim: Hand-written executable contracts from tools' advertised surfaces, checked statically and with dynamic probes, confirm seven tool defects in four benchmarks (incl. a MedAgentBench POST that reports success but never writes, and a tau2-bench cancel_reservation that never releases seats); recall on injected defects is low; findings and repairs were reported upstream as issues.
cite_claim: Benchmarks that grade tool-using agents assume tools do what they advertise; executable contracts found seven tool defects, including success messages for writes that never happened.
location: Abstract; Sec. on findings (Table IV); limitations
quote: the benchmarks certifying them grade what each simulated tool call reports having done, assuming the tool did what its interface advertises.
relevance: Independent evidence for fiks's read-after-write contracts and for M1 ('tools assumed correct'); real-bug candidates in tau2-bench/MedAgentBench/AgentDojo; artifact MIT on Zenodo. Not runtime, no F gate, no PR.

title: Skill Drift Is Contract Violation: Proactive Maintenance for LLM Agent Skill Libraries
authors: Linfeng Fan; Yuan Tian; Ziwei Li; Zhiwu Lu
central_claim: SkillGuard extracts executable environment contracts from skill documents and validates them against live evidence: 0 false alarms on 599 no-drift cases, 76% recall on known drift, 86% precision in a pre-registered live study of 49 skills; violated contracts raise one-round repair from 10% (2/20) to 78% (25/32), but the repaired object is the skill text and the verifier is literal.
cite_claim: Framing drift as contract violation gives precise maintenance signals and makes repair actionable.
location: Abstract; Sec. 4.1-4.3; Sec. 5.3; Appendix M Table 14; Appendix C
quote: Violated contracts also make repair actionable, improving one-round success from 10\% without localization to 78\%.
relevance: Closest research analogue of C19 ('the violated property localizes the repair'). Caveats from full text: unequal n (20 vs 32), gap vs plain drift text (60%) and self-refine (80%) not significant; behavioural assumptions explicitly out of scope. Shared key with gap-client-api-adaptation.

title: DepRepair: LLM-Based Source-Code Repair for Dependency Breaking Changes
authors: Shenghao Yang; Bo Lu; Yaochen Liu; Yu Kang; Qiongfang Zhang; Chetan Bansal et al.
central_claim: DepBench (95 real dependency-update breakages, 4 ecosystems, Docker oracle = consumer's own tests); DepRepair grounds repair in structured upstream evidence (89.5% with GPT-5.5); raw upstream evidence lowers pass rates by 7-23 pp; no failing test localizes the break.
cite_claim: Cross-repository breaking-change repair lacks a failing test that localizes the break, and raw upstream evidence hurts LLM repair while structured evidence helps.
location: Abstract; Sec. I; Sec. IV-A; Sec. V-E Table V
quote: no failing test localizes where the consumer breaks, leaving the repair under-informed.
relevance: Supports C19 (fiks supplies exactly the missing failing test) and creates a tension: 'raw upstream evidence hurts' vs fiks's raw-exchange trace. Categories are signature changes, not silent behaviour. Shared key with gap-client-api-adaptation.

title: DeltaMCP: Incremental Regeneration via Spec-Aware Transformation for MCP servers
authors: Aditya Pujara; Xiaogang Zhu; Hsiang-Ting Chen
central_claim: Given a new release of a service's OpenAPI spec, DeltaMCP regenerates only the affected MCP tools; evaluated on Azure REST API specs against full regeneration.
cite_claim: MCP-server maintenance under API evolution has been automated from spec diffs.
quote: DeltaMCP enables developers to only update the affected tooling of MCP servers, given a new release of it's corresponding service's OpenAPI specification.
relevance: Spec-triggered MCP repair (C27 cluster): cannot fire on fiks's drifts, whose spec is unchanged by construction. Baseline candidate if code is released [verify].

title: MCPEvol-Bench: Benchmarking LLM Agent Performance Across Dynamic Evolutions of MCP Servers
authors: Huanxi Liu; Kun Hu; Jiaqi Liao; Qiang Wang; Pengfei Qian; YuanZhao Zhai et al.
central_claim: 11 mutation operators derived from 515 servers / 9,273 versions simulate MCP tool evolution (tool, parameter and description changes) in 123 servers by editing server source; frontier models lose 13.7-14.4% task fulfillment; no repair method; release not stated.
cite_claim: MCP servers evolve continuously and frontier agents lose about 14% task fulfillment on evolved servers.
location: Abstract; Sec. 3; Sec. 5.2 Fig. 4; Sec. 6.2; Appendix B/E
quote: GPT-5.4 and Claude-Sonnet-4-6 exhibit performance declines of 13.7\% and 14.4\% in evolved MCP servers, respectively
relevance: Newest MCP drift benchmark; interface-level and backward-compatible by design, so it does not cover fiks's silent upstream drift (S-classes). Supports M1's claim that an upstream-changed/tool-unchanged benchmark is missing.

title: AgentBug-Smith: Automatically Reproducing Real-World Harness Bugs in Agentic Systems
authors: Yiming Cheng; Alfin Wijaya Rahardja; Mengshi Zhang; Zihao Chen; Zhenpeng Chen; Yiling Lou
central_claim: Automatically reproduces real-world harness bugs from open-source agent systems (10.67-27.56% higher reproduction success than general techniques) and builds Live-Harness-Bench with 200 reproducible bugs.
cite_claim: Real agent-system bugs can be continuously mined and turned into executable reproduction instances.
quote: turning real-world agent failures into executable evaluation instances and reusable knowledge for harness improvement
relevance: Issue-text-triggered reproduction (prose input) - the comparison arm for fiks's trace-vs-prose hypothesis; possible real-bug source.

title: AgentChaos: Chaos Engineering for Agent Systems via Programmatic Fault Injection
authors: Gou Tan; Zhensu Sun; Jieke Shi; Ting Zhang; Zilong He; Qingfu Wu et al.
central_claim: Runtime, non-intrusive fault injection at the HTTP layer of LLM APIs (crash, omission, value faults on content and tool-call fields); pass@1 drops up to 50 pts; existing fault diagnosis <53% accuracy on fault type.
cite_claim: HTTP-layer value-fault injection degrades agent systems by up to 50 points and existing diagnosis methods identify the fault type under 53% of the time.
quote: We define crash, omission, and value faults on content and tool call fields, intercept and modify LLM API responses at runtime
relevance: Fault-injection methodology close to fiks's vendor-api drifts but at the LLM-API layer, not the tool's upstream. Possible injector design reference.

title: Agents' Overreliance on Unreliable Tools
authors: Hoyeol Yang; Woojung Song; Taewon Kim; Jonghyun Song; Seoyeon Park; Yohan Jo
central_claim: Across 14 models and three tools with corrupted returns, agents adopt plausible-but-incorrect tool outputs at high rates (mean >1/3 per tool, 68.0% for web search) and rarely warn users; verification prompts partly help.
cite_claim: Agents adopt corrupted but plausible tool returns at high rates, up to 68% for web search.
quote: Agents adopt corrupted returns at high rates, with mean adoption exceeding one third for every tool and reaching 68.0% for web search.
relevance: Newer, broader evidence alongside C9 that silent wrong tool data propagates; motivates receipts.

title: Localizing Post-Wire Semantic Changes in MCP Agent Frameworks
central_claim: Differential testing of a fixed MCP tool result through four Python agent-framework integrations finds 13 fixture-task divergences in structured values, declared errors and rich content.
cite_claim: Agent frameworks alter or drop parts of valid MCP tool results (structured values, errors, rich content) after the wire.
quote: Valid Model Context Protocol (MCP) messages do not guarantee that an agent framework preserves the distinctions downstream software needs.
relevance: Threat to fiks's receipt delivery via _meta/structuredContent; supports the dual-channel (meta + text block) design and suggests a receipt-survival test per framework.

title: Can MCP Clients Decide What to Do After Failure? A Result-Only Actionability Audit
central_claim: In 21 induced failures from ten MCP servers, typed fields exposed failure in 18 but never a specific cause, target, executable repair or replay constraint.
cite_claim: MCP failure results rarely carry machine-readable recovery information.
quote: typed fields expose failure in 18 cases and a broad policy in 8, yet expose no specific cause, target, executable repair, or replay constraint.
relevance: Small-n support for receipts that name the violated property and recovery (fiks Rcpt).

title: Self-Healing Agentic Orchestrators for Reliable Tool-Augmented Large Language Model Systems
central_claim: Runtime orchestrator maps failure signals to classes and applies bounded recovery with verification; 98.8% success on a 100-task fault-injection benchmark; verifier-guided recovery cuts controlled semantic silent failures to 0%.
cite_claim: Runtime self-healing for agents (recovery, not tool repair) can suppress silent wrong outputs in controlled injection.
quote: Under a controlled semantic silent-failure setting, verifier-guided self-healing reduces silent failures to 0.0\%
relevance: Cluster D (runtime-only). Strongest 'detection/recovery suffices' counter-argument; it never changes the tool, so recurrence is unaffected (C12).

title: When Code Becomes an LLM Call: An Empirical Study of Call-Site Contracts in Agentic Systems
authors: Shihao Weng; Longtian Wang; Yang Feng; Mingfei Cheng; Jia Liu; Chao Shen et al.
central_claim: In 496 LLM call sites of 40 agentic systems, 63% of expected constraints are unmet and only 5.3% of call sites satisfy their whole contract; small code fixes enforcing the expected constraint stop all 38 runtime-triggered mechanisms.
cite_claim: Checks exist at most agent call sites but are usually inadequate; only 5.3% satisfy their full contract.
quote: Although 82% of call sites are checked before and after the call, 63% of the expected constraints are unmet
relevance: Supports 'presence of a check is not adequacy' - relevant to schema-only floors (X1) and to contract coverage limits.

title: Automated Program Repair Based on REST API Specifications Using Large Language Models
authors: Katsuki Yamagishi; Norihiro Yoshida; Erina Makihara; Katsuro Inoue
central_claim: dcFix detects REST API misuses in client programs against the API specification and repairs them with an LLM prompt that includes the non-conforming fragment and the spec.
cite_claim: LLM repair of client-side REST API misuse from specifications is established.
quote: dcFix identifies non-conforming code fragments, integrates them with the relevant API specifications into prompts, and leverages a Large Language Model (LLM)
relevance: Spec-conformance-triggered client repair; a follow-up (2608.29290) reaches 88.6% with RAG. Cannot target spec-invisible drift.

title: Incident-Arena: Getting agents to the last nine of reliability
authors: Andre Fu; Malik Drabla; Leon Liu; Meji Abidoye; Marek Suppa; Lata Mishra et al.
central_claim: 20 human-built incident-response tasks on real OSS deployed to ephemeral Kubernetes with injected faults and functional verifiers; frontier models score below 64.3%.
cite_claim: Agentic incident-repair benchmarks with functional verifiers show frontier agents below 64.3%.
quote: Across 20 tasks and 3 application substrates, frontier models score below 64.3%, with failures extending from diagnosis/localization errors, through incomplete repairs and unsafe regressions.
relevance: Evaluation-method reference for 'repair verified functionally, with no regressions'; loud faults, not silent.
